## How Extra Agents Create Value

Extra agents create value only when the split produces useful work that can be evaluated, selected, and integrated. The mechanism is not agent count. An extra agent must produce a candidate answer, piece of evidence, critique, memory update, tool action, branch, or routing decision that a cheaper baseline would not have produced as well. If that work is redundant, hard to check, or too costly to integrate, the extra agent is overhead.

This gives a simple answer to the reality check. Extra agents help by changing one of four variables in test-time computation: they widen the search frontier, reduce correlation among attempts, partition context or authority so workers can act without interfering, or move scarce judgment to the places where selection matters most. They hurt when the split creates more handoffs than evidence.

Wider search is the most basic source of value. Multiple agents can try different solution paths, retrieve different evidence, draft different patches, or run different experiments in parallel. This helps only when good candidates appear often enough and the system has a credible way to choose among them. Independent sampling and voting are the cleanest version: *More Agents Is All You Need* [@moreagents] shows that repeated agent executions can improve benchmark accuracy, but also makes the cost grow with ensemble size. Branch-and-merge software systems are the artifact-heavy version: CAID's gains come from isolated implementation attempts that can be committed, inspected, and merged, not from conversation alone [@caid].

Lower correlation is the second source. If every worker has the same model, prompt, context, and blind spot, additional agents mostly repeat the same trajectory. @agentscalingdiversity argue that scaling depends on effective independent channels rather than raw agent count: homogeneous systems saturate, heterogeneous systems help when they create complementary correct-path evidence, and diversity among wrong paths is not useful. @fig-diversity visualizes this effective-channel view of scaling. This explains why mixture and aggregation results are plausible but bounded. *Mixture-of-Agents* [@mixtureofagents] can improve generation when proposer models contribute complementary drafts to an aggregator; it is weaker evidence for general collaboration unless the same diversity and aggregation ablations hold in the target setting.

![Relationship between effective channel count K* and task accuracy in LLM multi-agent systems. Useful scaling comes from non-redundant, task-relevant evidence rather than raw agent count or superficial output diversity. Reproduced from @agentscalingdiversity.](figures/agent-scaling-diversity-kstar.png){#fig-diversity width=92% fig-alt="Plot relating effective diversity channels K star to accuracy in LLM-based multi-agent systems."}

Partitioning is the third source. Some tasks are too large, tool-specific, or stateful for one trajectory to handle cleanly. Extra agents can hold different context slices, use different tools, preserve separate memories, or work in separate artifact branches. The value is not that the agents have job titles. The value is that the split prevents interference while preserving enough provenance for later integration. Tool-specialized teams help when evidence or actions are naturally partitioned across browsers, terminals, files, APIs, or domain tools [@magenticone; @caid]. Shared-memory and delegation systems help when long-horizon state must outlive one context window, but they also create stale or poisoned state if memories are not sourced, repaired, and deleted.

Selection is the fourth source. Extra agents can serve as critics, judges, testers, reviewers, or managers who decide which work continues. Debate and critique help when reviewers expose errors that the original worker would not catch, but they can also converge on persuasive wrong answers [@du2023debate; @multiagentdebate]. Reflection-gated tool use, as in MIRROR, can catch some plan or tool-call errors before execution, while leaving hard constrained-planning tasks difficult [@mirror]. Human-governed portfolios are the strongest near-term form of selection: agents expand the menu of hypotheses, patches, experiments, and reviews, while humans spend attention on decomposition, taste, risk, and final merge decisions.

These mechanisms are heterogeneous, but not arbitrary. Wider search and lower correlation are inference mechanisms: they ask whether extra calls produce better candidates or evidence than serial reasoning, best-of-N, or voting. Partitioned context, durable delegation, and shared state are infrastructure mechanisms: they ask whether tools, files, permissions, logs, and memories let agents work without corrupting one another. Critique and human-governed portfolios are review mechanisms: they ask whether scarce judgment is aimed at the places where selection matters. Optimized coordination is a control mechanism: it asks whether routing, spawning, aggregation, stopping, and escalation can be learned or searched rather than hand-coded. @tbl-extra-agent-mechanisms turns this mechanism view into an audit checklist: for each proposed multi-agent gain, identify the work created by the split, the simpler baseline it must beat, and the failure mode that the split makes more likely.

| Mechanism | Work created by extra agents | Baseline to beat | Main failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wider search | More candidate answers, patches, plans, tests, or experiments | Budget-matched single agent, best-of-N, sampling and voting | More low-quality attempts than the verifier can reject |
| Less correlated evidence | Different models, prompts, tools, data slices, or memories expose complementary correct paths | Homogeneous ensemble with equal budget | Different-looking errors without useful evidence |
| Partitioned context and authority | Workers hold separate state, tools, permissions, or artifact branches | One long-context agent or fixed workflow | Orchestrator loses global state or merges incompatible work |
| Adversarial critique and checking | Reviewers, judges, testers, and reflectors catch local errors | Single-agent self-critique and extra-token controls | Persuasive wrong consensus or weak judging |
| Durable delegation | Memories, notes, commits, logs, and handoff records persist across workers | Larger context, retrieval, or ordinary project state | Stale, poisoned, or unsourced state |
| Human-governed portfolio | Humans choose among more evidence-rich alternatives | Human using one agent serially | Review bandwidth and integration become the bottleneck |
| Optimized coordination | Controller learns when to spawn, route, aggregate, stop, or escalate | Handcrafted topology and strong non-agentic workflow | Overfitting, reward hacking, brittle routing |

: Mechanism checklist for evaluating claims that extra agents create value. Each proposed gain should identify the extra work created by the split, the simpler baseline it must beat, and the failure mode the split makes more likely. {#tbl-extra-agent-mechanisms}

This mechanism view also clarifies when multi-agent systems are likely to hurt. They hurt when the task is tightly coupled, when the relevant evidence fits in one context, when validators are weak, when agents share the same blind spots, when messages are lossy, or when coordination cost exceeds the value of extra attempts. Multi-agent value must therefore be attributed to a specific mechanism that turns divided work into selected work, not to agent count. The next question is what survives from that work, in what form, and under what checks.
